   The memory-chip maker, a key partner to Nvidia, said market conditions and broader share-price trends drove the decision, and that the move doesn’t reflect any change in growth prospects for Solidigm, which was formed after SK Hynix’s acquisition of Intel’s NAND flash-memory business.

       Market Talk   From Dow Jones Newswires 

   The SEC Division of Examinations says that market participants using AI will be an area of focus going forward. The division, in its 2027 examination priorities, says it will focus on preparation for cyberattacks related to AI, which it refers to as “super intelligence,” as well as firms that use automated investment tools or trading algorithms. “When conducting these reviews, assessments generally will include whether: (1) representations are fair and accurate; (2) operations and controls are consistent with disclosures made to investors; and (3) algorithms lead to advice or recommendations consistent with investors’ investment profiles or stated strategies,” the division says. (Elias Schisgall, elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

   The outlook for Treasury yields “is highly dependent on Middle East conflict, Ukraine, Russia [and] potentially midterms,” DWS’s George Catrambone says. November’s election could determine the future of the war in Iran, which has been driving oil prices, he says. “Ultimately 10-year yields have been fairly well correlated to the price of oil.” Catrambone says the pace of investment on artificial intelligence infrastructure can also be affected by the midterms. Given the uncertainties, his investment strategy is “to be nimble.” Catrambone likes high-grade corporate bonds that are trading at a discount, while selectively adding lower quality yields aiming at a “strongly yielding portfolio and one that is diversified.” (Paulo Trevisani, paulo.trevisani@wsj.com)

An IPO Paused as AI Valuation Fears Mount
 
Plus, private equity’s healthcare playbook and family-friendly country clubs
 
 
KIM HONG-JI/REUTERS
 

SK Hynix has scrapped plans for a major U.S. public offering of its flash-memory subsidiary Solidigm, highlighting deepening investor caution toward artificial-intelligence valuations despite robust demand for AI-related hardware.

 

The memory-chip maker, a key partner to Nvidia, said market conditions and broader share-price trends drove the decision, and that the move doesn’t reflect any change in growth prospects for Solidigm, which was formed after SK Hynix’s acquisition of Intel’s NAND flash-memory business.

 

The Solidigm IPO would have raised funds for a new production facility in the U.S. to meet rising demand, SK Hynix said.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

The SEC Division of Examinations says that market participants using AI will be an area of focus going forward. The division, in its 2027 examination priorities, says it will focus on preparation for cyberattacks related to AI, which it refers to as “super intelligence,” as well as firms that use automated investment tools or trading algorithms. “When conducting these reviews, assessments generally will include whether: (1) representations are fair and accurate; (2) operations and controls are consistent with disclosures made to investors; and (3) algorithms lead to advice or recommendations consistent with investors’ investment profiles or stated strategies,” the division says. (Elias Schisgall, elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

 

The outlook for Treasury yields “is highly dependent on Middle East conflict, Ukraine, Russia [and] potentially midterms,” DWS’s George Catrambone says. November’s election could determine the future of the war in Iran, which has been driving oil prices, he says. “Ultimately 10-year yields have been fairly well correlated to the price of oil.” Catrambone says the pace of investment on artificial intelligence infrastructure can also be affected by the midterms. Given the uncertainties, his investment strategy is “to be nimble.” Catrambone likes high-grade corporate bonds that are trading at a discount, while selectively adding lower quality yields aiming at a “strongly yielding portfolio and one that is diversified.” (Paulo Trevisani, paulo.trevisani@wsj.com)
